**We already held the mechanism on a different operator, which is exactly why this needed measuring.** The catalog documents this first-operand rule on `NumberOfDifferentValues`, with its own worked pair — but a mechanism proved on one operator is not proved on another, the reuse needs no new branch, and so nothing prompts the question. `MaxValue`'s constraint named `MVK_NOT_SORTABLE` alone and `Min`'s said only "kinds cannot be mixed", so our own self-describing surface could not have told an author what `MaxValue(<date>, <number>)` would return. That gap is closed in the same change: all four entries now carry a `MVK_DATE_AND_NONDATE` corrective whose reject probe is CI-executed to that exact code and whose advertised repair is CI-executed as accepted.

*(Locked: `adapter.laws.ExtremaOperandFamilyRefusalLawsTest` — both leaders × both spellings × all four operators, with the family-homogeneous controls; plus the four catalog correctives, executed on both polarities by `CatalogExamplesAreKernelValidTest` and `CatalogKernelClaimEvidenceTest`.)*

## §6 supplement — the extractor gate and the opt-in pre-1900 policy on a CLOCK-DECLARED DATE, the carrier our read-gate table lacked (kernel `checkConsistency` + tri-engine, 2026-09-05) <a id="kf250"></a>

> Fold: pending — completes [KF211](#kf211)'s read-gate account on its missing carrier; folds into §6 on the next canonical KERNEL-SEMANTICS pass.

Takes the row a12-kernel-lean handed over from their `SPEC-2026-09-05-14` — so neither estate measured it twice — and settles, on the same model, a policy question they raised about six sites of theirs.

**The extractor pair, mirrored.** On a **DATE field declared `HH:mm:ss`**, `HoursFromTime` is **admitted** and `YearFromDate` is refused `MVK_WRONG_DATE_FORMAT_FOR_OP`; the admitted arm runs tri-engine, firing on `10:30:00` and silent on `11:30:00`. [KF211](#kf211)'s pair is the same two extractors with both axes flipped — admitted `YearFromDate`, refused `HoursFromTime`, on a TIME declared `yyyy-MM-dd`. Together the two carriers show the extractor gate keying on the declared format from **both** sides, which neither alone establishes.

**The opt-in pre-1900 guard is a model-ADMISSION question, and the answer is neither of the two an obvious 2×2 offers.** A DATE field declared `HH:mm:ss` carrying the check is refused outright — `MVK_ADDITIONAL_CHECK_INVALID`, *"For date fields without a year, no 'additional check' may be specified"* — while the identical check on a year-bearing DATE declaration is admitted and duly reports `datumFalsch` at `1899-12-31` and nothing at `1900-01-01`. So the guard is not admitted-and-inert on a clock declaration; it is **not declarable there at all**, and the kernel's own message keys on the declared format's components rather than on the kind. **Consumer consequence, which is why a12-kernel-lean asked:** a policy that admits the opt-in check for the DATE *kind* is over-permissive on exactly this declaration, and one that refuses it for the TIME and DATE_TIME kinds is right — but right by schema, not by kind-reasoning (below).

**The other half of that 2×2 names no model, so it is a SCHEMA fact.** `youngerThan1900Check` is a property of the **`DateType` declaration object**: the kernel's `TimeType` and `DateTimeType` carry `format` and annotations and nothing else (kernel SOURCE at 30.8.1, the primary oracle for a signature question). "A TIME field declared `yyyy-MM-dd` with the guard set" is therefore unrepresentable rather than refused. The one link source reading leaves open — whether the DM-JSON path would carry the key in anyway, making it declarable-but-inert — is attacked and closed: injecting it makes the kernel's own **deserializer** reject the model, naming `TimeType` and the property in its reference chain, one layer earlier than any consistency gate. So the shape never reaches a gate that could be inert.

**Our own builder will construct the refused model.** `dateField(…).format("HH:mm:ss").rejectBefore1900()` produces DM-JSON the kernel rejects at codegen; the diagnostic arrives from `checkConsistency` rather than from the builder. That is delegation under-reporting, which is safe rather than wrong. *Corrected 2026-09-05: this first deferred the disposition to the owner via a `DEV-API-GAPS` row. The class that row asked for was then enumerated — see [KF251](#kf251) — and the answer is that no client-side refusal is added, because the record a refusal would guard is also built on the READ path; the two codes carry a curated corrective instead.*

*(Locked: `adapter.laws.ClockDeclaredDateGateDiffTest` — the extractor pair with an ordinary-clock counterpart, the admitted arm run tri-engine on firing and non-firing documents, the admission refusal asserted as exactly one message with its code, the year-bearing control on both sides of the 1900 boundary, the model bytes asserted to carry the declarations each row needs, and the deserializer attack on the schema claim.)*

## §6 supplement — the two DateType CONFIG gates read the declared format differently, and the refusal echoes the format in German pattern letters (kernel `checkConsistency`, complete over the derived vocabulary, 2026-09-05) <a id="kf251"></a>

> Fold: pending — completes [KF250](#kf250)'s single measured pair into the class it belonged to; folds into §6 on the next canonical KERNEL-SEMANTICS pass.

[KF250](#kf250) measured **one** conflicting pair — a `HH:mm:ss`-declared DATE carrying the opt-in pre-1900 check — and left the class open. `DateType` carries exactly two config axes that can disagree with its declared format, so the class is finite: both are put to the kernel here against every format in the derived [temporal vocabulary](TEMPORAL-FORMAT-VOCABULARY.md), which is what makes the boundaries below component claims rather than one-spelling coincidences.

| config axis | the gate | admitted formats |
|---|---|---|
| `youngerThan1900Check` (`rejectBefore1900()`) | the declared format carries a **YEAR** | `yyyy`, `yyyy-MM`, `yyyyMM`, `yyyy-MM-dd`, `dd.MM.yyyy`, `yyyyMMdd`, `yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss` |
| a partial `datePrecision` (`DAY_`/`MONTH_`/`YEAR_OPTIONAL`) | the format is a **complete date and nothing further** | `yyyy-MM-dd`, `dd.MM.yyyy`, `yyyyMMdd` |

**The two gates disagree in both directions, which is why one pair could not have settled either.** `yyyy-MM` takes the guard and refuses the precision, so a refusal keyed on "the format is incomplete" over-rejects a model the kernel admits. And the instant format `yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss` takes the guard and **refuses the precision too, despite carrying all three date components** — so a refusal keyed on "the three components are present" would admit a model the kernel rejects. That cell was predicted ADMITTED here and measured refused; it is reachable rather than hypothetical, because the instant spelling is a legal DATE declaration ([KF206](#kf206) — the format gate reads the string, not the kind). The verdict does not move with *which* component a partial precision makes optional, and `FULL` — the default, never emitted — carries no format requirement at all, which is the control separating "a partial precision needs a complete format" from "declaring a precision at all needs one".

**A format that fails both gates draws both codes**, not the first: `MM-dd` + guard + partial precision reports `MVK_ADDITIONAL_CHECK_INVALID` and `MVK_OPTIONAL_DATE_TYPE_INVALID` together.

**The precision refusal echoes the offending format in GERMAN pattern letters, in every locale.** An `en_US` model declaring `yyyy-MM` is told *"A partial known date is not permitted for the format: `'JJJJ-MM'`"* — `y→J`, `d→T` (`MM-dd` → `'MM-TT'`, `MMdd` → `'MMTT'`, `HH:mm:ss` unchanged). A `de_DE` model produces the identical spelling, which is the discriminator: this is a fixed letter substitution, **not** a localization, so no reader ever sees the format they must actually declare. An author who copies the spelling out of the diagnostic writes a format the kernel refuses outright.

**Disposition — the corrective, not a client-side refusal.** Both codes are orphans of the operator catalog-join (no operator's `invalidExample` documents a field-declaration conflict), so each now carries a curated `fix`/`explain` in `StructuralKernelFix`, naming the formats that *would* be accepted and warning off the German spelling. A client-side refusal was measured, considered and declined: `FieldTypeSpecReader` builds `DateSpec` on the **read** path, so a constructor check would make an inconsistent-but-present kernel model unreadable rather than merely unauthorable, and a builder-only check would cover `DateFieldBuilder` while missing the CLI's own authoring path. Delegation already reports both conflicts correctly; what was missing was the corrective, which is the enricher's lane.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.TemporalDeclarationConfigAdmissionLawsTest` — both grids over the complete admitted vocabulary, the bare-declaration and `FULL` positive controls, the both-axes conflict, the two refusal messages pinned verbatim, the German-letter substitution across two locales and four formats, and the enrichment asserted through `KernelDiagnostics.enriched` — the exact call `model check` makes. The class is a registered completeness claimant of `TemporalFormatVocabularyGuardTest`, so a short axis fails the build rather than narrowing the basis silently.)*

## §6 supplement — the DATEFRAGMENT kind admits the SAME twelve formats, measured rather than inherited (kernel `checkConsistency` over the derived candidate universe, 2026-09-05) <a id="kf252"></a>

> Fold: pending — extends [KF206](#kf206)'s kind-independence onto the one date-bearing kind its grid never covered; folds into §6 with it.

[KF206](#kf206) established that the temporal format gate reads the string and not the kind, over **DATE / TIME / DATE_TIME**. `DateFragmentType` was outside that grid — it declares its format under its own key (`formatOfFragment`) — and every surface in this estate named the same four members for it (`MM`, `yyyy`, `yyyy-MM`, `MM-dd`), including [KF81](#kf81)'s own bullet. Measured over the [derived candidate universe](TEMPORAL-FORMAT-VOCABULARY.md): **all twelve admitted formats are admitted on a fragment field too**, `yyyy-MM-dd`, `dd.MM.yyyy`, `yyyyMMdd`, `HH:mm:ss` and the ISO instant included.

**Why it needed measuring instead of extending.** A fragment is *by definition* a date that is not a full calendar date, so a narrower set was the plausible reading, and extending KF206 to it would have been a scope transfer onto an unmeasured carrier — the failure the four-member lists in three published schema descriptions and the diagnostic enricher actually exhibited. The domain now regenerates from the kernel as its own section of the derived artifact, beside the DATERANGE pair table, so no consumer assembles it from the members it happened to use.

**The limit, stated because a reader will otherwise carry the result further than the measurement.** This is an **admission** result only. The fragment RUNTIME completion recorded in §6 ("date-fragment runtime completion" — missing month/day to `01`, missing year from the Base Year) was measured on the four conventional formats; what a fragment declared `yyyyMMdd` — a *complete* date wearing the fragment kind — does at runtime is unmeasured on either engine, and the interpreter's `DatePrecision.FRAGMENT` path has never seen that combination. *Settled 2026-09-05, same day: measured across all three routes — comparison against a full date, paired comparison between two fragments of one declaration, and the formal check that runs with no rule reading the value — the two engines agree everywhere, because a clock-declared fragment is handled as a clock value rather than through the fragment completion ([IF327](INTERPRETER-FINDINGS.md#if327)).*

*(Locked: `validate.laws.TemporalFormatVocabularyGuardTest` — the fragment probe is a third derived domain with its own discrimination floor, and the artifact comparison fails the build if the kernel and the committed set disagree.)*

## §9 supplement — `NumberOfDifferentValues` counts temporal operands by DECODED date, so two spellings of one date count once (adapter differential, 2026-09-05) <a id="kf253"></a>

> Fold: pending — the runtime half of [KF193](#kf193)'s temporal aggregate gate; folds into §9 beside [KF226](#kf226) on the next canonical pass.

[KF193](#kf193) measured `NumberOfDifferentValues`'s *admission* gate: date-like operands must share a declared component SET, not a format string, so `yyyy-MM-dd` beside `dd.MM.yyyy` is admitted. That admission is what makes this question askable at all — the two operands can hold **different stored texts denoting one date**, and there a textual identity and a chronological one give different counts. Measured on both engines: the count is **chronological**.

| operands | stored values | distinct count |
|---|---|---|
| `yyyy-MM-dd`, `dd.MM.yyyy` | `2024-03-05`, `05.03.2024` — one date, two spellings | **1** |
| `yyyy-MM-dd`, `dd.MM.yyyy` | `2024-03-05`, `06.03.2024` — different dates | 2 |
| `yyyy-MM-dd`, `yyyy-MM-dd` | `2024-03-05`, `2024-03-05` | 1 |
| `yyyy-MM-dd`, `yyyy-MM-dd` | `2024-03-05`, `2024-03-06` | 2 |

**The first row alone does not establish it, and that is the whole design of the table.** A count of 1 is equally consistent with a decoded comparison and with an engine that cannot evaluate a cross-spelling pair and folds it to one value — the two are indistinguishable from a single cell. The second row holds the spelling difference fixed and varies only whether the dates agree; the collapse reading cannot produce its 2. The same-spelling pair is the third leg, showing a count of 1 is reachable through the path nobody disputes, so neither arm is a constant.

**Read against its neighbour or the result inverts.** `FieldValuesNotUnique` refuses this pair outright at authoring under its own code, so it never reaches a runtime identity question — do not carry either operator's answer to the other ([KF226](#kf226) records the same warning on the classification gate). No Base Year is declared in the measured model: every declaration carries its own year, so supplementation is not a second variable here.

**Asked by a12-kernel-lean's `SG22`**, whose `route-state` recorded the question as having no constructible witness — "under a mandatory single format the decoded and stored accounts agree on every currently constructible input". The premise is what fails: the format is not mandatory-single for *this* operator, which is exactly the fact their proposed format-equality gate would have erased. They have withdrawn the recommendation.

*(Locked: `adapter.laws.DistinctCountTemporalIdentityDiffTest` — every cell asserts kernel and interpreter equal before its value is pinned, so an engine divergence fails ahead of the pin; the cross-spelling pair's admission is asserted rather than assumed, since a refused pair would make the counts measurements of a model that does not exist.)*

## §6 supplement — the temporal format gate is CASE-SENSITIVE, and "lowercase" was never the rule (kernel `checkConsistency` over a new case axis, 2026-09-05) <a id="kf254"></a>

> Fold: pending — closes the case axis [KF206](#kf206)'s string-gate result left unprobed; folds into §6 with it.

Eleven published schema descriptions and the diagnostic enricher all said a date/time format must be **"a LOWERCASE Java pattern"**. Read literally that licenses `yyyy-mm-dd`, which the kernel refuses. Measured over a new case axis — both the all-lowercase and all-uppercase spelling of every candidate, universe 135 → 375: **no case variant of any admitted format is accepted**, and the admitted set stays exactly twelve.

| spelling | verdict |
|---|---|
| `yyyy-mm-dd`, `yyyymmdd`, `dd.mm.yyyy`, `hh:mm:ss` | REFUSED |
| `YYYY-MM-DD`, `YYYYMMDD` | REFUSED |
| the twelve as published | ADMITTED |

**"Lowercase" was reaching for a real fact and named the wrong one.** The surfaces carry a true adjacent claim — the A12 editor's UPPERCASE labels (`YYYY-MM-DD`) are display labels, not format values — and "lowercase" was shorthand for *not those*. But the actual rule is that Java pattern letters are case-**significant**: `MM` is months where `mm` is minutes, so `yyyy-mm-dd` is a **different pattern**, not a miscased one. A reader who applied the description's own rule produced a string the description's own list does not contain.

**The mechanism is the one this file keeps recording: a description asserted a rule no candidate exercised.** The generator varies components and separators — the axis [KF196](#kf196) proved discriminating — at fixed case throughout, so both case claims were unfalsifiable by construction. That is the same defect as the short allowlists [KF252](#kf252) corrected, one layer up: there the *set* was wrong, here the *rule for forming a member* was, and neither was reachable by the probe that was supposed to cover the surface. Adding the axis was the fix; rewording alone would have left the next case claim equally unchecked.

**Found by a12-kernel-lean, 2026-09-05**, who read the schema before the diagnostic, wrote the lowercase spelling and lost a round to it — the failure mode the description uniquely causes, since `field add`'s own rejection text was correct and lists all twelve. Their report is what prompted the axis; the verdicts above are measured here.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.TemporalFormatVocabularyGuardTest` — the case axis is generated from every candidate rather than from named members, so a future admitted format is case-probed without anyone remembering to add it.)*

## §11 supplement — the operand-scope law transfers to the RULE carrier unchanged, sibling index rows included (kernel `checkConsistency`, 2026-09-06) <a id="kf255"></a>

> Fold: pending — completes [KF226](#kf226)-era carrier discipline on the §11 scope law; folds into §11 beside the computation rows.

`ComputationOperandScopeLawsTest` established on the **computation** carrier that an operand is admitted by whether the target's repetition scope **binds** every repeatable level it crosses — not by scope equality, and not by cross-group-ness. Whether a **rule** decides the same way was an explicitly unmeasured transfer. Measured now: **it does, on every row, including the three that make the law interesting.**

| operand, relative to the error field | rule carrier | computation carrier |
|---|---|---|
| form-level into a one-level / two-level target | ADMITTED | ADMITTED |
| one level up into a two-level target | ADMITTED | ADMITTED |
| own level — control | ADMITTED | ADMITTED |
| one level BELOW the target | `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` | `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` |
| repeatable into a form-level target | `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` | `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` |
| sibling repeatable, index field SAME name | ADMITTED | ADMITTED |
| sibling repeatable, index field ANOTHER name | `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_INVALID_INDEX` | `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_INVALID_INDEX` |
| sibling repeatable, NO index field | `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` | `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` |

**A clean transfer is a result, not a non-result, and it had to be run rather than assumed.** This estate has measured the opposite outcome three times in a week on one operator family ([KF120](#kf120), [KF218](#kf218), [KF242](#kf242)) — the reuse needs no new branch, so nothing prompts the question and a silent assumption that happens to hold produces no signal at all. The row that would have been most expensive to get wrong is the sibling triple, where siblinghood alone predicts one verdict and the kernel gives three.

**The two carriers are NOT symmetric, which is what made the transfer non-obvious.** A rule's condition must reference its error field (`MVK_ERROR_FIELD_NOT_REFERENCED`), so every rule row carries **two** operands where the computation rows carried one, and the error-field read is itself a scope participant. A computation can pair a bare constant with a repeating target; a rule cannot. The scope verdict is nevertheless identical, so the binding relation is decided by the operand and the target locus alone and does not count operands.

**Vacuity is excluded by the sibling table rather than by a separate control**: one helper returns three distinct outcomes over three groups differing only in their index declaration, so it is demonstrably reading the kernel and not defaulting.

**Prompted by a12-kernel-lean's `SG5`**, which reframed its own row around this boundary rather than assuming it after their cross-group probe turned out to be the no-index-field case. The result closes the transfer for both estates; the carrier boundary is now measured rather than flagged.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.RuleOperandScopeLawsTest` — the computation law's fixture verbatim, so the carrier is the only variable; each table pinned as measured.)*

## §9 supplement — a FILTERED star is an admitted operand at every entity-list carrier, and the temporal gate reads through the filter (kernel `checkConsistency`, 2026-09-06) <a id="kf256"></a>

> Fold: pending — extends [KF193](#kf193)'s temporal gate and [KF125](#kf125)'s slot laws onto the filtered operand shape; folds into §9.

Nothing in this estate had crossed `Having` with the extremum operators — six law files use `.having(…)` and none reached `MaxValue`/`MinValue` or `latestOf`/`earliestOf`. Measured now, on our own fixture: **a filtered star is admitted wherever a plain star is**, and the temporal component-set gate still runs on it.

| operand shape | verdict |
|---|---|
| temporal extremum, plain star — control | ADMITTED |
| temporal extremum, FILTERED star | ADMITTED |
| numeric extremum, plain star — control | ADMITTED |
| numeric extremum, FILTERED star | ADMITTED |
| `NumberOfDifferentValues` / `FieldValuesNotUnique`, filtered star (each with its plain-star control) | ADMITTED |
| filtered star **beside a differing component set**, both in the operand list | `MVK_DATEFORMATS_NOT_COMPATIBLE` |
| filtered star beside the same set spelled differently | ADMITTED |

**Our pre-checks were silent here, not deliberate.** `ListAggregate` and `DateListAggregate` inspect an operand's KIND and never its filter, so a filtered star built through `FieldListRef.having(…)` passed straight through. That is the correct behaviour — but "delegated on purpose" and "nobody looked" are indistinguishable from inside the code, and only a run separates them. This is the read-path half of the client-refusal rule arriving as its mirror image: the risk was never a wrong refusal, it was an untested absence of one.

**The refusal row is what stops the admissions being worthless.** Six ADMITTED cells are equally well explained by "a filtered operand is not gate-checked at all" — a worse outcome than a refusal, since it would mean the filter smuggles an operand past the temporal gate. The differing-set row shows the gate still fires through the filter.

**A first draft measured the wrong gate, and its own control caught it.** Putting the second date on the **comparison** rather than in the operand list made every row ADMITTED — correctly, because an aggregate compared to a date is a *direct* comparison and takes §6's coarse gate (year presence, date/no-date class), while the exact component-set gate reads the aggregate's own operand list. Published as-is it would have claimed "the filter exempts the operand from the gate". The plain-star control failed by being ADMITTED where it had no business being: a control earns its place by failing when the row's **design** is wrong, not only when the kernel surprises you.

**Prompted by a12-kernel-lean**, whose own decline of this shape rested on a *real* neighbouring divergence — the DATERANGE-endpoint carrier genuinely refuses starred operands under `MVK_NO_WILDCARDS_ALLOWED`. A known-real boundary predicted the wrong side of itself, which is a stronger argument for measuring than an unsupported guess would have been.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.FilteredStarExtremumOperandLawsTest` — every filtered row carries its plain-star control, and the numeric extremum sits beside the temporal one so a refusal would separate a filtered-star ban from a temporal-carrier one.)*

## §11 supplement — a wrong-kind CONSTANT assignment reports an ordered ladder over the (constant, target) PAIR (kernel `checkConsistency` via raw `DraftComputation`, 2026-09-06) <a id="kf257"></a>

> Fold: pending — a §11 authoring-tier diagnostic law; folds into §11 beside the computation kind rows.

Which class the kernel reports for a wrong-kind constant assignment is **not** a function of the target kind, and not of the constant either. It is an ordered ladder over the pair, measured here on one model carrying a target of every kind:

| rung | condition | class |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | target is BOOLEAN | `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_YESNO`, for **any** constant |
| 1 | target is CONFIRM | `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_YES`, for **any** constant |
| 2 | constant is TEMPORAL, any remaining target | `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_DATE` — String and Number included |
| 3 | otherwise the target decides | temporal → `..._TO_DATE`; String/Enum → `..._TO_ENUM_OR_STRING`; NUMBER → `..._TO_ENUM_OR_STRING` for a string constant but **`MVK_INCONSISTENT_TYPES_COMPARED`** for a Boolean one |

**Two cells are pair-dependent and the rest are target-keyed, which is exactly what makes a careless sample dangerous.** A batch that holds the constant fixed and varies the target produces a clean target-keyed table *whether or not the target is the key* — the assumption is not merely unverified there, it is unfalsifiable by that batch. Both exceptions are locked against same-target controls carrying a different constant, so the pair-dependence is visible rather than inferred: rung 2's temporal column, and the Boolean-into-NUMBER cell where one target yields two classes.

**BOOLEAN and CONFIRM do not share a class.** They sit at the same rung and report different codes, so a checker collapsing the two flag kinds is wrong on one of them.

**A "temporal literal" is not a separate syntax — it is a string literal whose CONTENT parses as a date.** The kernel lexer admits one spelling (`StringLiteral : '"' ( '""' | ~["] )* '"'`, cited in our own `DslRenderer`), so `"05.03.2024"` is temporal and `"pending"` is not, by content alone. Single quotes are not a literal and draw `MVK_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN` — which is how a mis-spelled probe row silently leaves the grid instead of failing: a first draft here spelled the string constant `'pending'` and four cells reported a parse error that looked like data. A bare `05.03.2024` lexes as a Number, pinned by its own row.

**None of this is authorable through our typed surface** — `Computation.Builder`'s kind/format gate refuses every cell first, with a kind-mismatch message that names no code. That is correct behaviour and not a defect: the kernel refuses all of them too, so the pre-check is delegation-equivalent, merely earlier. It does mean the kernel's own class was unmeasured here, reachable only through the raw `DraftComputation` seam that `ConfirmComputationSourceKindLawsTest` established for the same reason.

**The ladder is the kernel's COMPARISON vocabulary, not an assignment table — corrected the same day.** The identical class fires on a plain rule condition with no computation and no assignment anywhere (`[Handler] == "05.03.2024"` on a String field), with the non-date literal at that exact site admitted as the control; The `Having` filter is the third carrier and is measured here too — a12-kernel-lean reported it first, and it is re-derived on our fixture because our shipped corrective names it, so it may not rest on their run. **Hypothesis, not a finding:** that assignment reaches this gate through its generated equality rule, which would explain why the codes are named `..._COMPARE_TO_...` at all. Both estates reached that account independently and neither holds a witness for it — concurrence tests whether two parties reason alike from the same input, never whether the account is right. The discriminator nobody has built: a case separating a generated equality rule from a classifier that both routes simply call. It matters beyond taxonomy: the first version of our corrective was written from the assignment carrier alone and spoke of a "target" — a word with no referent in a filter or a plain comparison. That is the same comparison-versus-assignment split that had left the ledger rows incomplete, repeated one level out, inside the fix for it.

**Consequence taken:** `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_DATE` now carries a `StructuralKernelFix` corrective telling the author to check the LITERAL before the field, since the code fires against fields with nothing temporal about them and on every carrier. Three MVK-ledger rows classified `erased` were extended in place — they described the *comparison* surface, and assignment is a second, live firing site on it.

**Reported by a12-kernel-lean (`LF153` / `SPEC-2026-09-06-03`)**, whose own account rests on 80 kernel-gated children in one batch; re-derived here on our fixture rather than cited, because our diagnostic surface is what carries the corrective. Their method note is the transferable part: *name the key you think the answer is a function of, and vary it* — if the honest answer is "left, right, or the pair", cross them.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.LiteralComparisonDiagnosticLadderLawsTest` — each rung with its same-target controls, plus the bare-dotted-literal fixture control. Open here as there: a CUSTOM target, the one rung the ladder does not claim.)*

## §9 supplement — the exact-duplicate gate reads a reference's FORM, so a starred operand may repeat where a direct one may not (kernel `checkConsistency`, 2026-09-06) <a id="kf258"></a>

> Fold: pending — sharpens the duplicate-slot rows in §9; folds beside [KF125](#kf125).

`MVK_DUPLICATE_PARAM1` rejects an *exact* reference repeated in one operand list — and "exact" is load-bearing. A **wildcarded (starred) occurrence is a repetition-wide scan rather than an exact reference**, so two of them are two independent reads and repeat legally:

| operand list | verdict |
|---|---|
| `AtLeastOneFieldValueIncludedInValueList(Code, Code In …)` | `MVK_DUPLICATE_PARAM1` |
| `AtLeastOneFieldValueIncludedInValueList(Items*/Sku, Items*/Sku In …)` | ADMITTED |
| `NumberOfValueInFields(0 In Total, Total)` | `MVK_DUPLICATE_PARAM1` |
| `NumberOfValueInFields(0 In Items*/Count, Items*/Count)` | ADMITTED |
| two *distinct* direct references, either carrier — liveness control | ADMITTED |

**Our catalog said this on seven operators and contradicted it on two.** `Sum`, `MaxValue`, `MinValue`, `NumberOfDifferentValues`, `NumberOfFilledFields`, `NumberOfFilledGroups` and `FirstFilledValue` all spell out the star exemption. The value-list family said only "no exact reference may repeat" and `NumberOfValueInFields` said "a field may not be listed more than once" — both of which, read as written, forbid a form the kernel admits. That is an **internal contradiction in one shipped artifact**, which is what makes it a defect rather than a difference of emphasis: an author reading one entry gets a rule the neighbouring entry denies. Both corrected.

**The liveness control is what makes the admissions mean anything.** Without a distinct-reference row on each carrier, "the starred repeat is admitted" and "this operator never reaches the duplicate gate at all" are the same observation; the direct-duplicate row then shows the gate is armed in the same model.

**Reported by a12-kernel-lean on four carriers** (value list, `NumberOfDifferentValues`, `FieldValuesNotUnique`, `Sum`). Measured here on the two whose *wording* was wrong, since our published text is what carried the defect — the other two already said the right thing. Their same-day corroboration from the other direction is **their report and not re-derived here**: at the DateRange overlap operators a keyed reference repeated under the *same* key refuses and under a *different* key is admitted, which would make the exact identity the (field, key) pair.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.StarredOperandRepeatExemptionLawsTest` — both carriers, each with its direct-duplicate row and its distinct-reference liveness control.)*
